```{r setup}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(rnaturalearth)
library(glmmTMB)
library(broom.mixed)
library(here)

panel  <- read_csv(here("data", "processed", "bt_climate_panel.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
models <- readRDS(here("output", "models.rds"))
```

## Question

Are warmer-than-usual years associated with more bluetongue outbreaks in European countries?
Bluetongue is a vector-borne disease of ruminants transmitted by *Culicoides* midges, whose
activity and range are expected to respond to temperature.

## Data

- **Outbreaks:** official bluetongue outbreak notifications from the EU Animal Disease
  Information System (ADIS), aggregated by country and year. Country-years with no notified
  outbreak are set to zero.
- **Climate:** annual temperature anomalies per country relative to 1991–2020, from Our World
  in Data, derived from the Copernicus ERA5 reanalysis.

```{r data-summary}
panel |>
  summarise(countries = n_distinct(iso3),
            years = paste(min(year), max(year), sep = "–"),
            total_outbreaks = sum(outbreaks),
            share_zero = scales::percent(mean(outbreaks == 0)))
```

## Outbreaks over time

```{r time-series}
panel |>
  group_by(year) |>
  summarise(outbreaks = sum(outbreaks), temp_anomaly = mean(temp_anomaly, na.rm = TRUE)) |>
  ggplot(aes(year, outbreaks)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c7fb8") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Notified outbreaks (all study countries)",
       title = "Bluetongue outbreaks notified to ADIS per year") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Where outbreaks were reported

```{r map}
europe <- ne_countries(scale = "medium", continent = "Europe", returnclass = "sf") |>
  select(iso3 = iso_a3_eh, geometry)

totals <- panel |> group_by(iso3) |> summarise(outbreaks = sum(outbreaks))

europe |>
  left_join(totals, by = "iso3") |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = outbreaks), colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log1p", na.value = "grey90", name = "Outbreaks") +
  coord_sf(xlim = c(-12, 35), ylim = c(34, 71)) +
  labs(title = "Total bluetongue outbreaks notified, by country") +
  theme_void()
```

## Model

Outbreak counts are over-dispersed, so a Poisson model is not appropriate. I fitted a
negative-binomial mixed model:

`outbreaks ~ temperature anomaly + year trend + (1 | country)`

The country random intercept absorbs stable differences between countries, such as livestock
population, surveillance intensity and reporting practice. The year trend captures changes over
time that are not linked to temperature, such as vaccination campaigns.

```{r model-compare}
AIC(models$pois, models$nb, models$nbmm)
```

```{r model-table}
tidy(models$nbmm, effects = "fixed", conf.int = TRUE, exponentiate = TRUE) |>
  select(term, IRR = estimate, conf.low, conf.high, p.value) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), \(x) round(x, 3)))
```

The incidence rate ratio (IRR) for `temp_anomaly` is the multiplicative change in expected
outbreaks for a +1 °C annual anomaly, holding country and trend constant.

*Write 3–4 sentences here once the model has run: the IRR with its confidence interval, whether
the association is clear or uncertain, and what the country effects suggest.*

## Limitations

- **Reporting bias.** Notified outbreaks reflect surveillance and reporting effort as well as
  disease. The country random effect only handles differences that are stable over time.
- **Vaccination and serotypes.** Large vaccination campaigns and new serotype incursions
  (for example BTV-8 in 2006–2008 and BTV-3 from 2023) drive outbreaks strongly and are not
  modelled here.
- **Coarse climate data.** A national annual anomaly hides seasonal and local conditions that
  matter for *Culicoides*; monthly, sub-national data would be more appropriate.
- **Association, not causation.** This is an ecological analysis at country-year level.

## Next steps

Monthly and sub-national ERA5 data, vector habitat covariates, serotype and vaccination
information, and spatio-temporal models (for example INLA) would make the analysis much
stronger. WAHIS data would extend it beyond the EU.
